items.title: What "Self" Actually Means: A Convenient Fiction, Not a Real Thing

items.zh: 又我今當說第一義我相。所言我者，唯於諸法假立為有，非實有我。然此假我、不可說言與彼諸法異不異性。勿謂此我是實有體，或彼諸法即我性相。
items.en: I shall now state the ultimate mark of the self. What is called "self" is merely provisionally posited upon phenomena as existing — it is not a truly, substantially existing self. Yet this provisional self cannot be said to be either the same as, or different from, those phenomena. One should not suppose this self has a truly existing substance, nor suppose that those phenomena themselves simply are the self's own nature.

items.zh: 又此假我是無常相，是非恒相，非安保相，是變壞相，生起法相，老病死相，唯諸法相，唯苦惱相。故薄伽梵說：苾芻當知！於諸法中，假立有我。此我無常無恒，不可安保，是變壞法，如是廣說。
items.en: Further, this provisional self bears the mark of impermanence; the mark of not enduring; the mark of being insecure; the mark of being subject to change and decay; the mark of arising only as a dependent phenomenon; the mark of ageing, sickness, and death; the mark of being merely a succession of conditioned phenomena; and the mark of being merely suffering. Hence the Blessed One said: "Monks, you should know that within phenomena, a self is provisionally posited. This self is impermanent, does not endure, is not secure, is subject to change" — and so on in full detail.

items.zh: 由四因故，於諸行中假設有我。一、為令世間言說易故，二、為欲隨順諸世間故，三、為欲斷除謂定無我諸怖畏故，四、為宣說自他成就功德、成就過失、令起決定信解心故。是故執有我論，非如理說。
items.en: For four reasons, a self is provisionally posited upon the formations. First, to make worldly communication easy. Second, to accord with worldly convention. Third, to remove the fear that arises from thinking there is definitely no self at all. Fourth, to teach how beings, oneself and others, come to possess virtues or faults, so as to give rise to firm, settled conviction. It is for this reason that the doctrine holding a real self to exist is not a soundly reasoned teaching.

items.title: The Fifth Doctrine: A Self and World That Are Simply Permanent

items.zh: 計常論者，謂如有一，若沙門、若婆羅門，起如是見，立如是論：我及世間皆實常住，非作所作，非化所化，不可損害，積聚而住，如伊師迦。
items.en: The doctrine positing permanence: there are certain renunciants or brahmins who hold such a view and establish such a doctrine — that the self and the world are both truly permanent, neither made by any maker nor transformed by any transformer, incapable of being harmed, standing firm as an accumulated mass, like the Īṣīkā.

items.zh: 謂計前際說一切常者、說一分常者，及計後際說有相者、說無相者，說非想非非想者，復有計諸極微是常住者，作如是計。
items.en: This is held by those who, examining the prior extremity of time, speak of everything as permanent, or of a portion as permanent; by those who, examining the latter extremity of time, speak of a persisting perception, of no perception, or of neither perception nor non-perception; and, further, by those who hold that atomic particles themselves are permanent.

items.zh: 問：何故彼諸外道起如是見，立如是論：我及世間是常住耶？答：彼計因緣，如經廣說，隨其所應盡當知。

items.title: Why They Believed This: Misread Meditative Memory, and Mistaking Atoms for Ultimate Reality

items.zh: 此中計前際者，謂或依下中上靜慮起宿住隨念，不善緣起，故於過去諸行，但唯憶念，不如實知，計過去世以為前際，發起常見。或依天眼，計現在世以為前際，於諸行剎那生滅流轉不如實知。
items.en: As for those who look to the prior extremity of time: some, relying on lesser, middling, or superior meditative concentration, give rise to memory of past abodes, and, being unskilled regarding dependent origination, merely recollect past formations without genuinely understanding them, and so posit the past as a prior extremity, giving rise to a view of permanence. Others, relying on the divine eye, take the present as a prior extremity, failing to genuinely understand that formations arise and cease moment to moment in continuous flow.

items.zh: 又見諸識流轉相續，從此世間至彼世間無斷絕故，發起常見。或見梵王隨意成立，或見四大種變異，或見諸識變異。
items.en: Further, some, seeing consciousness flow on in unbroken succession from this world to the next, give rise to a view of permanence on that basis. Others see Brahmā bring beings into being at will; others see the four great elements undergo change; others see consciousness undergo change.

items.zh: 計後際者，於想及受雖見差別，然不見自相差別。是故發起常見，謂我及世間皆悉常住。
又計極微是常住者，以依世間靜慮起如是見。由不如實知緣起故，而計有為先，有果集起，離散為先，有果壞滅。由此因緣，彼謂從眾微性，麁物果生，漸析麁物，乃至微住；是故麁物無常，極微是常。
items.en: Further, those who hold atomic particles to be permanent arrive at this view by relying on worldly meditative concentration. Not genuinely understanding dependent origination, they suppose that atoms exist first, and gross objects then arise as their combined result; and that when atoms disperse, the gross object that resulted is destroyed. On this basis, they hold that gross objects arise from an assembly of atomic particles, and that analysing a gross object down and down eventually reaches the abiding atom itself — and so conclude that gross objects are impermanent while the atom alone is permanent.

items.title: The Efficient Refutation: Permanence Is Just "Self" Again, Already Defeated

items.zh: 此中計前際後際常住論者，是我執論差別相所攝故。我論已破，當知我差別相論亦已破訖。
items.en: As for those who, looking to the prior or the latter extremity of time, hold a doctrine of permanence: this is included among the differentiated forms of the doctrine positing a self. Since the doctrine of self has already been refuted, it should be understood that its differentiated forms have thereby already been refuted as well.

items.zh: 又我今問汝，隨汝意答。宿住之念，為取諸蘊？為取我耶？若取蘊者，執我及世間是常，不應道理。
items.en: Further, I now ask you, answer as you see fit: does memory of past abodes take the aggregates as its object, or does it take a self as its object? If it takes the aggregates as its object, then insisting that a self and world are thereby proven permanent makes no sense.

items.title: Memory Recalls Only the Aggregates, and No Single Consciousness Stays Constant

items.zh: 若取我者，憶念過去如是名等諸有情類，我曾於彼如是名、如是姓乃至廣說，不應道理。又汝意云何？緣彼現前和合色境眼識起時，於餘不現不和合境所餘諸識，為滅？為轉？
items.en: If it takes a self as its object, then recalling that beings in the past bore such-and-such a name, such-and-such a lineage, and so on in full detail, while claiming "I was that one" — this makes no sense, since what is recalled is always these particular, changing details, never a bare self. Further, what do you think: when eye-consciousness arises, taking as its object present, conjoined visible form, do the remaining forms of consciousness — not presently active, their objects not conjoined — cease, or do they continue?

items.zh: 若言滅者，滅壞之識而計為常，不應道理。若言轉者，由一境界、依一切時一切識起，不應道理。
items.en: If you say they cease, then calling a consciousness that has ceased and perished "permanent" makes no sense. If you say they continue, then having a single object give rise to every kind of consciousness at every single moment makes no sense either — this plainly contradicts direct experience.

items.title: Perception and Feeling Constantly Vary — So Whatever Bears Them Cannot Be Changeless

items.zh: 又汝何所欲？所執之我，由想所作及受所作，為有變異？為無變異？若言有者，計彼世間及我常住，不應道理。若言無者，有一想已，復種種想，復有小想及無量想，不應道理。又純有樂已，復純有苦，復有苦有樂，有不苦不樂，不應道理。
items.en: Further, what do you actually intend: does the self you posit, insofar as it is shaped by perception and by feeling, undergo change, or not? If it does, then claiming the world and the self are thereby permanent makes no sense. If it does not, then having a single, undifferentiated perception at one time and manifold perceptions at another — narrow perception here, boundless perception there — makes no sense. And having purely pleasant feeling at one time, purely painful feeling at another, a mixture of both at a third, and neither pleasant nor painful at a fourth, likewise makes no sense for something that supposedly never changes.

blocks.text: Having refuted a real self, the treatise now says what "self" does mean: a convenient designation, used for good reasons. This short passage is one of the clearest statements of the Buddhist two-truths approach to the self. Then the fifth doctrine begins: that self and world are permanent.

Untranslated: 0307c09–c11 (why outsiders hold permanence: "their reasons are as explained at length in the sūtras") and 0307c18–c21 (those who reckon the future, seeing differences in perception and feeling but not differences in their own nature, form the view that self and world are permanent).

"What is called 'self' is merely provisionally posited upon phenomena as existing; it is not a truly, substantially existing self." This provisional self "cannot be said to be either the same as or different from" the phenomena. Master Cháng Bǎi: it is named on the aggregates, so it is not different from them; but the aggregates are real processes with their own substance while the self has none, so it is not the same.

The provisional self has the marks of the aggregates: impermanent, not enduring, insecure, subject to change, arising only on conditions. So when we say "I", we speak truly, provided we mean a changing stream and not an owner behind it.

subs.head: Four reasons to speak of a self

blocks.text: Why use the word at all? Four reasons:

items: "to remove the fear that arises from thinking there is definitely no self at all";
to show how oneself and others gain virtues and faults, and so to give rise to firm conviction in karma.

blocks.text: Master Cháng Bǎi on the third: "Some, hearing 'no self', become terrified and can no longer practise; telling beings there is a self that does good and evil is a provisional teaching." Non-self is not nihilism, and a teacher must not frighten people away from the path with it. This is worth remembering when explaining Buddhism to new students.

The fifth doctrine: "the self and the world are both truly permanent, neither made by any maker nor transformed by any transformer, incapable of being harmed, standing firm … like the Īṣīkā." Venerable Miào Jìng gives two readings of Īṣīkā: a very firm mountain near Rājagṛha, or a very tough grass. Ru-Yi combines them.

Master Cháng Bǎi: the view usually arises from two sources, concentration and reasoning. Meditators who recall past lives see continuity and conclude something permanent continues; "outsiders can attain absorption, but without Buddhist wisdom they misjudge what they see." Others, seeing Brahmā apparently established at will (Day 10), conclude he is permanent though others are not. Others, by reasoning, decide atoms are permanent.
The lesson for meditators: experiences in meditation need wisdom to interpret them. A real experience can support a false view.

First, permanence of the self is just the self-doctrine again, already refuted. Second, memory of past lives recalls "a being of such a name and lineage", that is, aggregates, never a bare self. Third, no consciousness stays constant: when eye-consciousness takes an object, the others are not all active. Venerable Miào Jìng quotes the *Great Learning*: "When the mind is absent, one looks without seeing, eats without tasting." Fourth, perception and feeling constantly vary, narrow in the desire realm and boundless in the form realm, so whatever bears them cannot be changeless.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what is the ultimate mark of the self?
options: merely provisionally posited on phenomena, not a real self; this provisional self can be called neither the same as nor different from them
quiz.why: "What is called 'self' is merely provisionally posited upon phenomena as existing — it is not a truly, substantially existing self. Yet this provisional self cannot be said to be either the same as, or different from, those phenomena." Having refuted a real self, the treatise keeps a provisional one for ordinary speech.

quiz.q: Why can the provisional self be called neither the same as nor different from the aggregates?
options: because the self is named on the aggregates, it isn't different; but the aggregates are dependent and have substance while the self has none, so it isn't the same
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Named on form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness … one can't say the self differs from the aggregates"; "yet this self is not a conditioned dharma with substance, only a designation, so one can't say they're the same." Venerable Miào Jìng: "The aggregates are dependent in nature … they have substance; the self has none." (The reading note reverses the *Pixunji*'s pairing — logged in the correction list.)

quiz.q: According to the treatise, for what four reasons is a self provisionally posited on the formations?
options: to ease communication; to accord with convention; to remove fear of "no self at all"; to teach how oneself and others gain virtues or faults, giving rise to firm conviction
quiz.why: "First, to make worldly communication easy. Second, to accord with worldly convention. Third, to remove the fear that arises from thinking there is definitely no self at all. Fourth, to teach how beings, oneself and others, come to possess virtues or faults, so as to give rise to firm, settled conviction." Master Cháng Bǎi: if one only ever said "no self," people wouldn't believe — the provisional self accords with them.

quiz.q: The third reason is "to remove the fear of thinking there is definitely no self." How does Master Cháng Bǎi explain it?
options: some, hearing "no self," become terrified and can't practice; telling them a self does good and evil is a provisional teaching
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Some, hearing 'no self,' become terrified and can no longer practice; telling beings there is a self that does good and evil is a provisional teaching." Venerable Miào Jìng: to those attached, "definitely no self" is frightening; to remove that fear, a self is spoken of.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what does the doctrine of permanence hold?
options: self and world are truly permanent — not made by a maker, not transformed by a transformer, unharmable, standing firm like the Īṣīkā
quiz.why: "The self and the world are both truly permanent, neither made by any maker nor transformed by any transformer, incapable of being harmed, standing firm … like the Īṣīkā." Master Cháng Bǎi: "not transformed" means not conjured by Maheśvara, Brahmā, or other powerful beings. Two main branches: a permanent self, and permanent atoms.

quiz.q: According to Master Cháng Bǎi, from what two situations does the view of permanence usually arise?
options: through concentration or through reasoning — outsiders attain absorption but lack Buddhist wisdom, so they misjudge what they see
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Two situations usually cause this attachment: one is concentration, the other reasoning"; "outsiders can attain absorption, but without Buddhist wisdom they misjudge what they see and form wrong views." Venerable Miào Jìng: those holding it are not the distracted but "people with absorption and supernormal powers" — yet powers are unreliable.

quiz.q: Does memory of past lives take the aggregates or a self as object? If a self, why does it fail?
options: what is recalled is a being of such a name and lineage — differences of aggregates, never a bare self
quiz.why: "If it takes a self as its object, then recalling that beings in the past bore such-and-such a name, such-and-such a lineage … makes no sense." Venerable Miào Jìng: "That recalls only names and lineages — not a self; how could it take a self?" If it takes the aggregates, they're impermanent and prove nothing permanent.
